To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fetal DNA fraction in maternal blood is a function of the fetal fraction and the fetal DNA fraction, and that the fetal DNA and fetal DNA fractions can be predicted from the maternal DNA fraction.

the fetal fraction in maternal plasma was higher in the first trimester than in the second trimester, and that the fetal fraction was higher in the second trimesters of twin pregnancies than in the singletons.
we developed a new technique for the detection of fetal DNA in the maternal blood and that this method is more sensitive and specific than other methods.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and analysis of free fetal DNA in maternal blood and the application of this to the noninvasive prenatal diagnosis of fetal aneuploidy.
the development of methods for the recovery and analysis of fetal DNA from the maternal circulation.
the identification and characterization of a novel protein that is highly expressed in the developing mouse embryo and in a subset of human cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current methods of noninvasive prenatal testing using cell-free DNA are not sufficiently reliable to be used in the general population.
the percentage of free DNA is not a reliable marker of the presence of a fetus with a genetic disease.
the use of free fetal DNA in maternal plasma for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis of fetal aneuploidy is feasible, reliable, safe, and cost-effective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our results suggest the presence of a large number of novel miRNAs in the human placenta.

we are able to recover a higher amount of free fetal DNA from the maternal circulation by increasing the amount of blood drawn from the mother and using the DNA extraction method with the highest yield.
we are able to increase the percentage and amount of free fetal DNA in maternal plasma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of fetal DNA in a sample is not the most important factor in determining whether a sample will be informative for a noninvasive test.
the use of a single cell-free DNA sample for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis is feasible.
the use of a single cell type to model the human immune system is unlikely to be sufficient. 2018. 2019; 10: 1-11. doi:10.1186/s13075-019-1907-x.
